stances.claim: The SCS arbitral ruling should be elevated to the UNGA for enforcement -- but not during the current regime. The UNGA is structurally favorable: 145 of 193 members are littoral states whose Unclos benefits (12-mile territorial sea, 200-mile EEZ, 350-mile continental shelf) align with the PH win; the US, UK, and other great powers will support because the ruling upheld freedom of navigation and overflight; and a UNGA endorsement would make China 'a rogue state, a pariah' under international public-opinion pressure.

FS Teodoro Locsin Jr.'s rejection -- 'We won already, why would you want to relitigate something that you already won... Once you throw it to the UN, I'm afraid China has the numbers there and it's about numbers. It's not about law' -- carries weight because Locsin was previously PH's UN ambassador and has 'done a reality check on how to win in the world body.'

Reality 1: UNGA members 'do not always vote according to law, reason, or logic'; they often decide 'according to politics and compromise, and exchange favors via the diplomatic quid pro quo, known in street lingo as scratch my back and I will scratch yours' -- and Locsin may have 'run out of favors to exchange' or judged that PH cannot match the quid-pro-quo China can offer.
stances.rhetorical_move: quid-pro-quo realism with pop-culture reference (Madam Secretary)

stances.claim: Reality 2: SCS-bordering countries -- even those with claims conflicting with China's -- do not automatically side with PH because they weigh other dependencies; Brunei imports 'a huge amount' of its crude oil from China, 'the backbone of its economy,' which a Chinese cutoff could 'severely imperil.' These countries may simply adopt China's counter-arguments: (1) ruling void for lack of jurisdiction (land-features dispute, not maritime rights); (2) tribunal didn't rule on China's ownership of land features; (3) unlike ICJ decisions, the arbitral ruling 'is not part of international law and has no precedent value.'

The Chinese counter-arguments 'can be overcome. Surely.' -- but given Locsin's 'unyielding stance,' the prudent course is to wait for a new regime after the 2022 elections 'that may hopefully be gung-ho in using all its diplomatic weapons -- reason, logic, law, politics, compromise, back-channeling, and quid pro quo, plus old-fashioned grit and the perseverance to win.' Otherwise, 'to insist now may result in the tragic and irreversible loss of what we already won.'

notable_anecdotes: The 'Madam Secretary' Netflix reference -- 'For more vivid samples of quid pro quo, watch Madam Secretary on Netflix' -- CJ's uncharacteristic pop-culture pull-in, used to make diplomatic quid pro quo concrete for general readers.

The Brunei-crude-oil dependency vignette -- 'a huge amount of Brunei's crude oil -- the backbone of its economy -- is imported by China. Should the latter stop or minimize its imports, Brunei's economy may be severely imperiled' -- physicalizing how Chinese leverage operates on littoral-state diplomacy without need for naval threat.

Locsin's quoted rejection in full register -- 'We won already, why would you want to relitigate something that you already won... I'm afraid China has the numbers there and it's about numbers. It's not about law' -- capturing the foreign secretary's blunt skepticism in his own voice.

The three-part China counter-argument inventory -- (1) jurisdiction-void claim, (2) land-features-not-ruled-on claim, (3) arbitral-vs-ICJ-precedent claim -- modeling exactly the legal-diplomatic ground PH would need to recapture in any UNGA push.

The 'world's largest maritime military exercises' US move 'a few weeks ago' -- anchoring the comparative-power tilt: the US is already enforcing the ruling unilaterally, providing implicit pressure that complements any UNGA elevation.
The 145-of-193 littoral-state arithmetic -- converting 'logically and reasonably they would vote in favor' into a defensible arithmetic prediction rather than a hope.

The closing seven-weapon diplomatic toolkit -- 'reason, logic, law, politics, compromise, back-channeling, and quid pro quo, plus old-fashioned grit and the perseverance to win' -- taxonomic compression of what a post-2022 'gung-ho' regime would need to deploy.

The tragic-irreversibility warning -- 'to insist now may result in the tragic and irreversible loss of what we already won' -- the precise downside specification that justifies CJ's strategic patience.

one_paragraph_summary: To the question whether the Philippines should elevate the 2016 South China Sea arbitral ruling upholding its maritime rights to the United Nations General Assembly for enforcement, Panganiban answers 'Yes, but not now, not during this regime.' The UNGA is the best forum: a joint statement by former Foreign Secretary Albert Del Rosario and retired SC Justices Antonio T. Carpio and Conchita Carpio Morales argued that 145 of the 193 UNGA members have ocean and sea borders -- and would 'logically and reasonably' vote to enforce the ruling because doing so reaffirms the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which extended their territorial sea from 3 to 12 miles, recognized their 200-mile exclusive economic zone, and their continental shelf of up to 350 miles. The US, UK, and other great powers will support the move because the ruling upheld freedom of navigation and overflight in the SCS -- the US (though a non-Unclos signatory) has already begun unilateral enforcement, conducting 'the world's largest maritime military exercises' there a few weeks before the column. But 'not now,' because FS Teodoro Locsin Jr. -- previously PH ambassador to the UN, so qualified to 'do a reality check on how to win in the world body' -- rejected the proposal: 'We won already, why would you want to relitigate something that you already won... Once you throw it to the UN, I'm afraid China has the numbers there and it's about numbers. It's not about law.' CJ unpacks two realities: (1) UNGA members 'do not always vote according to law, reason, or logic' -- they exchange favors via diplomatic quid pro quo ('scratch my back and I will scratch yours'; 'For more vivid samples of quid pro quo, watch Madam Secretary on Netflix'), and Locsin may have 'run out of favors to exchange' or believe PH cannot match China's quid pro quo; and (2) SCS-bordering countries weigh their claims against other dependencies -- 'a huge amount of Brunei's crude oil -- the backbone of its economy -- is imported by China,' so a Chinese cutoff could 'severely imperil' it. These countries may adopt China's counter-arguments: (1) the ruling is void for lack of jurisdiction because the dispute was over land features, not maritime rights; (2) the tribunal didn't rule on Chinese ownership of the land features and the Philippines didn't dispute it; and (3) unlike ICJ decisions, the arbitral ruling 'is not part of international law and has no precedent value.' These can be overcome -- 'Surely' -- but given Locsin's 'unyielding stance,' CJ recommends waiting for a new regime after the 2022 elections that may be 'gung-ho in using all its diplomatic weapons -- reason, logic, law, politics, compromise, back-channeling, and quid pro quo, plus old-fashioned grit and the perseverance to win.' Otherwise, 'to insist now may result in the tragic and irreversible loss of what we already won.'
